source.text: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֡וּא יִפְקֹ֣ד יְהוָה֩ בְּחַרְב֨וֹהַקָּשָׁ֜ה וְהַגְּדוֹלָ֣ה וְהַֽחֲזָקָ֗ה עַ֤ל לִוְיָתָן֙ נָחָ֣שׁ בָּרִ֔חַ וְעַל֙ לִוְיָתָ֔ן נָחָ֖שׁ עֲקַלָּת֑וֹן וְהָרַ֥ג אֶת־הַתַּנִּ֖ין אֲשֶׁ֥ר בַּיָּֽם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: In the day the that will visit Yahweh with his sword the fierce and the great and the mighty on Leviathan, a snake fleeing, and on Leviathan, a snake twisting, and he will slay the monster that [is] in the sea.

en.L: In that day {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will punish with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} sword, the hard and the great and the strong, Leviathan the fleeing serpent, \q and Leviathan the twisting serpent, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will kill the monster that [is] in the sea.
en.B: On that day {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will take {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} great sword, harsh and strong, and bring it down on Leviathan the serpent in flight, \q on Leviathan the coiling serpent; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will kill the monster that lives in the sea.
en.R: At that time {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will use {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} powerful sword to punish Leviathan. \q Leviathan is the snake that slips away, the snake that twists and coils. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will kill that great monster in the sea.

decisions.choice: Leviathan: the sea serpent of ancient Near Eastern stories, here the figure for every power that opposes God
alternatives: a symbol of a particular nation (Assyria, Babylon or Egypt)
decisions.reason: Leviathan is a monster of the sea in the poetry of the Old Testament (Job 3:8; 41:1; Psalm 74:14; 104:26). Texts from ancient Ugarit, written centuries before Isaiah, tell of the storm god Baal striking a seven-headed sea serpent called Lotan, described with the same two words as here, "fleeing serpent" and "twisting serpent". Isaiah uses the old picture to say that the LORD, not any other god, will defeat chaos and evil at the end. The name is kept at every level.

decisions.choice: fleeing ... twisting: the serpent that slips away and the serpent that coils
alternatives: three different monsters, each a nation
decisions.reason: The first word describes something that flees or glides swiftly (Job 26:13, of a serpent God pierced); the second means crooked or winding. Some readers see two monsters, or three with the sea monster, standing for different empires; the parallel lines more likely describe one creature from different sides.

decisions.choice: the monster in the sea: the sea dragon, as in 51:9
decisions.reason: The same word names the sea monster God defeated in 51:9 and Psalm 74:13; Ezekiel 29:3 uses it for Pharaoh. The verb "punish" here is the one used in 24:21 and 26:21 for God's coming to judge.

decisions.choice: Leviathan is the snake that slips away ... that great monster
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the list into short sentences and repeats the name of the LORD as the subject of the last one, so the reader knows who kills the monster.

records.literal_gloss: In the day the that, a vineyard of delight, sing of it.

en.L: In that day, \q a vineyard of delight, sing of it!
en.B: On that day, \q sing of a vineyard of delight!
en.R: At that time, \q sing a song about a lovely vineyard!

decisions.choice: a second song of the vineyard, answering the song of 5:1-7
decisions.reason: In 5:1-7 the vineyard was Israel and Judah; it bore bad grapes, and God let it be trampled and overrun with thorns and briers. This song reverses that one: God guards the vineyard, has no anger against it, and its fruit fills the world (verse 6).

decisions.choice: a vineyard of delight (the Masoretic Text)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text reads "delight", as in "vineyards of delight" in Amos 5:11. Some Hebrew manuscripts have a word that differs by one similar letter and means "foaming wine", giving "a vineyard of wine" (compare Deuteronomy 32:14). Both describe a vineyard at its best.

decisions.choice: sing of it: a call to more than one singer; "it" is feminine
decisions.reason: The verb is plural, calling the listeners to take up the song. The pronoun "it" is feminine, though "vineyard" is usually masculine; it may point beyond the vineyard to the people or the city it stands for.

source.text: אֲנִ֤י יְהוָה֙ נֹֽצְרָ֔הּ לִרְגָעִ֖ים אַשְׁקֶ֑נָּה פֶּ֚ן יִפְקֹ֣ד עָלֶ֔יהָ לַ֥יְלָה וָי֖וֹם אֶצֳּרֶֽנָּה׃

records.literal_gloss: I Yahweh [am] its keeper, every moment I water it, lest should visit on it, night and day I guard it.

en.L: I, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, [am] its keeper; \q at every moment I water it; \q lest [anyone] harm it, \q night and day I guard it.
en.B: I, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, am the one who tends it. \q I give it water moment by moment. \q So that no one will do it harm, \q I stand guard over it night and day.
en.R: I, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, take care of this vineyard. \q I water it again and again. \q I watch over it night and day so that no one will hurt it.

decisions.choice: keeper: the one who guards and tends the vineyard
decisions.reason: The word means one who watches over something (Job 27:18, a watchman's hut in a vineyard). God himself does the work that a hired keeper would do. In 5:6 he withheld rain; here he waters it.

decisions.choice: harm it: the verb of verse 1, here for an attack on the vineyard
decisions.reason: The verb in verse 1 means God coming to punish; here it means someone coming against the vineyard to damage it. God will punish Leviathan, but no one will be allowed to punish his vineyard.

source.text: חֵמָ֖ה אֵ֣ין לִ֑י מִֽי־יִתְּנֵ֜נִי שָׁמִ֥יר שַׁ֨יִת֙ בַּמִּלְחָמָ֔ה אֶפְשְׂעָ֥ה בָ֖הּ אֲצִיתֶ֥נָּה יָּֽחַד׃

records.literal_gloss: Rage there is not to me; who will give me thorns, briers in battle? I will march against it, I will burn it altogether.

en.L: Wrath there is none in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. \q Who would give {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} thorns [and] briers in battle? \q I would march against it; I would burn it all together.
en.B: There is no anger in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. \q If only thorns and briers stood against {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} in battle! \q I would advance on them and burn them all at once.
en.R: I am no longer angry with {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} vineyard. \q If thorns and briers rose up to fight {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, I would march out against them and set every one of them on fire.

decisions.choice: I have no anger: God's anger against his vineyard is over
decisions.reason: In 5:5-6 God turned against the vineyard in judgment. Now he says he has no anger toward it (compare 12:1; 54:8-9). Any anger left is turned against what would harm the vineyard.

decisions.choice: who would give me: a way of expressing a wish, "if only"
decisions.reason: "Who will give?" is a common Hebrew way of saying "if only" (Deuteronomy 5:29; Psalm 14:7). God wishes the thorns and briers would come out to fight him, because he would easily destroy them.

decisions.choice: thorns and briers: the weeds of 5:6, here standing for the vineyard's enemies
alternatives: the vineyard itself, if it again bore thorns
decisions.reason: The same pair overran the abandoned vineyard in 5:6 (also 7:23-25; 9:17; 10:17). Here they stand for whatever would choke or attack the vineyard, and God would burn them like dry brush. "It" (feminine) takes the thorns and briers together.

decisions.choice: them (Balanced and Readable) for "it"
decisions.reason: The Hebrew "it" gathers the thorns and briers into one; the plural makes clear what God would burn.

decisions.choice: no longer ... with my vineyard
decisions.reason: Readable names the vineyard and adds "no longer" to show the contrast with 5:1-7.

source.text: א֚וֹ יַחֲזֵ֣ק בְּמָעוּזִּ֔י יַעֲשֶׂ֥ה שָׁל֖וֹם לִ֑י שָׁל֖וֹם יַֽעֲשֶׂה־לִּֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Or let him take hold of my protection, let him make peace with me, peace let him make with me.

en.L: Or let [him] take hold of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} stronghold; \q let him make peace with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}; \q peace let him make with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.
en.B: Or else let them take hold of {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} as their stronghold. \q Let them make peace with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}; \q peace with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} let them make.
en.R: The other choice is for them to hold on to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} for protection \q and make peace with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. \q Yes, they should make peace with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: or let him: the enemy, pictured as the thorns, is offered another way
decisions.reason: The singular "him" refers back to the enemy of verse 4. Instead of being burned, he may seek shelter with God and make peace. The offer stands open even to those who opposed the vineyard.

decisions.choice: my stronghold: God as a place of refuge
decisions.reason: The word means a fortress or place of safety (25:4; Psalm 27:1; 31:3). To take hold of it is to rely on God's protection.

decisions.choice: peace ... peace: the call is repeated in reverse order for emphasis
decisions.reason: The second line reverses the first ("make peace with me, peace make with me"), which presses the invitation home.

decisions.choice: them (Balanced and Readable) for "him"
decisions.reason: The singular stands for the enemy as a group, the thorns and briers of verse 4.

source.text: הַבָּאִים֙ יַשְׁרֵ֣שׁ יַֽעֲקֹ֔ב יָצִ֥יץ וּפָרַ֖ח יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וּמָלְא֥וּ פְנֵי־תֵבֵ֖ל תְּנוּבָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: The coming [days], will take root Jacob, will blossom and bud Israel, and they will fill the face of the world [with] fruit.

en.L: [In days] to come Jacob will take root; \q Israel will blossom and sprout, \q and they will fill the face of the world [with] fruit.
en.B: In the days ahead Jacob will put down roots; \q Israel will flower and send out shoots, \q and they will cover the face of the world with fruit.
en.R: In the days to come, the people of Jacob will be like a plant that puts down deep roots. \q Israel will bloom and grow new branches. \q Their fruit will cover the whole world.

decisions.choice: the coming [days]: a time still ahead
alternatives: those who come (Jacob will cause them to take root)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "the coming ones"; "days" is understood. Another reading takes it as "those who come", the people who come back (verse 13), as the subject of "will take root".

decisions.choice: the vineyard bears fruit at last, enough to fill the world
decisions.reason: In 5:2-4 the vineyard bore only stinking grapes. Here Israel flourishes, and its fruit reaches the whole world, as in 2:2-3, where the nations come to learn from God (compare Hosea 14:6-8).

decisions.choice: the people of Jacob will be like a plant
decisions.reason: Readable says that Jacob means the people and makes the picture of a plant explicit.

source.text: הַכְּמַכַּ֥ת מַכֵּ֖הוּ הִכָּ֑הוּ אִם־כְּהֶ֥רֶג הֲרֻגָ֖יו הֹרָֽג׃

records.literal_gloss: Like the blow of the one striking him has he struck him? Or like the slaughter of his slain has he been slain?

en.L: Like the striking of the one who struck him has {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} struck him? \q Or like the slaughter of his slain has he been slain?
en.B: Has {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} struck Jacob the way {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} struck the one who struck him? \q Or has Jacob been slain the way his slayers were slain?
en.R: Has {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} punished Israel as hard as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} punished Israel's attackers? \q Has Israel been killed the way {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} killed those who killed them? No!

decisions.choice: two questions expecting the answer no: God has not struck Israel as hard as its enemies
decisions.reason: "He" who strikes is God, and "him" is Jacob, the people (verses 6 and 9). God's blows on Israel were measured (verse 8), but on Israel's attackers they were final.

decisions.choice: his slain: those who slew him, or those slain on his account
alternatives: the slaughter God dealt out for Israel
decisions.reason: The phrase is short and can be read more than one way: "the slaughter of his slain" may mean the slaughter that fell on Israel's killers, or the slaughter of those God killed for Israel's sake. Either way, Israel's enemies suffered worse than Israel.

decisions.choice: Jacob (Balanced); the LORD, Israel (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has only pronouns. Balanced names Jacob from verse 6; Readable names both the LORD and Israel, and adds "No!" to give the answer the questions expect.

source.text: בְּסַּאסְּאָ֖הבְּשַׁלְחָ֣הּ תְּרִיבֶ֑נָּה הָגָ֛ה בְּרוּח֥וֹ הַקָּשָׁ֖ה בְּי֥וֹם קָדִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: By measure, by sending her away you contended with her; he removed [her] by his wind the fierce in the day of the east wind.

en.L: By measure, by sending her away, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} contended with her; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} removed [her] by {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} harsh wind in the day of the east wind.
en.B: In due measure, by sending her away, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} contended with her; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} swept her off with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fierce blast on the day the east wind blew.
en.R: You punished {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} people in a measured way, by sending them away from their land. \q God drove them out with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} strong breath, like the hot wind from the east.

decisions.choice: by measure: the punishment was limited
decisions.reason: This word occurs only here. It looks like a doubled form of the word for a dry measure (a seah), "measure by measure", meaning that God set limits on Israel's punishment. Others take it from a sound used to drive animals away, "by driving her out".

decisions.choice: sending her away: exile pictured as a husband sending away his wife
decisions.reason: The verb "send away" is used for divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1; Isaiah 50:1), and "her" is the people pictured as a woman. God's case against her ended in exile, not destruction.

decisions.choice: the east wind: the hot, dry wind from the desert
decisions.reason: The east wind blows in from the desert, withering plants (Genesis 41:6; Hosea 13:15). It pictures the force with which God drove the people from the land. The verse changes from "you" to "he", as Hebrew poetry often does when speaking of God.

decisions.choice: your people ... from their land; God drove them
decisions.reason: Readable says who "her" is and where she was sent, and names God for "he".

source.text: לָכֵ֗ן בְּזֹאת֙ יְכֻפַּ֣ר עֲוֺֽן־יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְזֶ֕ה כָּל־פְּרִ֖י הָסִ֣ר חַטָּאת֑וֹ בְּשׂוּמ֣וֹ׀כָּל־אַבְנֵ֣י מִזְבֵּ֗חַ כְּאַבְנֵי־גִר֙ מְנֻפָּצ֔וֹת לֹֽא־יָקֻ֥מוּ אֲשֵׁרִ֖ים וְחַמָּנִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: Therefore by this will be atoned for the iniquity of Jacob, and this [is] all the fruit of removing his sin: when he makes all the stones of altar like stones of chalk pulverized, will not stand Asherahs and incense altars.

en.L: Therefore by this the iniquity of Jacob will be atoned for, \q and this [is] all the fruit of the removing of his sin: \q when he makes all the stones of the altar like chalkstones crushed to pieces, \q Asherah poles and incense altars will not stand.
en.B: So by this Jacob's guilt will be covered over, \q and this is the full harvest that comes from taking his sin away: \q he will make every altar stone like chalk crushed to powder, \q and no Asherah pole or incense altar will be left standing.
en.R: This is how the sin of Jacob's people will be forgiven and taken away. \q They will smash every stone of their false altars until it is like chalk crushed into dust. \q No poles for the goddess Asherah and no altars for burning incense will be left standing.

decisions.choice: will be atoned for: the guilt is covered and removed
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for atonement in the law (Leviticus 16:30) and in 6:7, where the prophet's sin is atoned for. Here the guilt is dealt with "by this", the measured punishment of verses 7-8, which leads the people to destroy their idols.

decisions.choice: he makes: Jacob, who breaks up the idolatrous altars
decisions.reason: The subject is Jacob, the people. The fruit of their forgiveness is that they tear down their own altars to other gods, as faithful kings did (2 Kings 23:4-15).

decisions.choice: Asherah poles and incense altars: objects of worship of other gods
decisions.reason: Asherah was a Canaanite goddess, and wooden poles set up in her honor stood beside altars (Deuteronomy 7:5; Isaiah 17:8). The incense altars served the same worship.

decisions.choice: They will smash ... their false altars
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that the people destroy the altars and that the altars were for false gods; the plural follows "Jacob's people".

source.text: כִּ֣י עִ֤יר בְּצוּרָה֙ בָּדָ֔ד נָוֶ֕ה מְשֻׁלָּ֥ח וְנֶעֱזָ֖ב כַּמִּדְבָּ֑ר שָׁ֣ם יִרְעֶ֥ה עֵ֛גֶל וְשָׁ֥ם יִרְבָּ֖ץ וְכִלָּ֥ה סְעִפֶֽיהָ׃

records.literal_gloss: For a city fortified [is] alone, a habitation deserted and forsaken like the wilderness; there grazes a calf, and there it lies down, and it consumes its branches.

en.L: For the fortified city [is] solitary, \q a dwelling sent away and forsaken like the wilderness; \q there the calf grazes, and there it lies down, and it eats bare its branches.
en.B: For the walled city sits alone, \q a home left empty and abandoned like the desert. \q Calves graze there; there they lie down and strip its branches bare.
en.R: The strong city with high walls is empty. \q No one lives there anymore. It is as deserted as the desert. \q Young cattle eat grass there and lie down there. They eat the leaves off its trees.

decisions.choice: the fortified city: left unnamed, as in 24:10, 25:2 and 26:5
decisions.reason: The city is not named. Some take it as the enemy's city, set against Israel's renewal in verse 6; others take it as a city of Jacob, since verse 11 speaks of a people its Maker will not pity (compare 1:3). The picture of cattle grazing in a ruin is used for Judah in 5:17 and 17:2.

decisions.choice: sent away: emptied of its people
decisions.reason: The word is from the verb "send away" in verse 8: the city has been driven out like the people.

source.text: בִּיבֹ֤שׁ קְצִירָהּ֙ תִּשָּׁבַ֔רְנָה נָשִׁ֕ים בָּא֖וֹת מְאִיר֣וֹת אוֹתָ֑הּ כִּ֣י לֹ֤א עַם־בִּינוֹת֙ ה֔וּא עַל־כֵּן֙ לֹֽא־יְרַחֲמֶ֣נּוּ עֹשֵׂ֔הוּ וְיֹצְר֖וֹ לֹ֥א יְחֻנֶּֽנּוּ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: When dry up its branches they are broken off; women coming setting light to it; for not a people of understanding [is] it; therefore not will have compassion on it the one who made it, and the one who formed it not will show favor to it.

en.L: When its boughs dry up they are broken off; \q women come [and] set fire to them. \q For it [is] not a people of understanding; \q therefore the one who made it will not have compassion on it, and the one who formed it will not show it favor.
en.B: When its boughs dry out they snap off, \q and women come and use them to light their fires. \q For these people have no understanding. \q So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} who made them will feel no pity for them; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} who shaped them will show them no kindness.
en.R: When the branches dry out, they break off. \q Then women come and use them for firewood. \q These people do not understand. \q So God, who made them, will not have mercy on them. The one who formed them will not be kind to them.

decisions.choice: not a people of understanding: they do not know their God
decisions.reason: The words recall 1:3, "my people do not understand", and Deuteronomy 32:28. Lack of understanding means refusing to know and follow God, not lack of intelligence.

decisions.choice: the one who made it ... the one who formed it: God the Creator withholds pity
decisions.reason: Elsewhere Isaiah calls God the one who made and formed Israel as a reason for comfort (43:1; 44:2). Here the Maker himself withholds compassion, which shows how serious the people's failure is.

decisions.choice: it: the people of the city
decisions.reason: The pronoun is masculine singular and refers to "people"; Balanced and Readable use the plural.

decisions.choice: God, who made them
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the maker so the reader does not mistake who is meant.

source.text: וְהָיָה֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֔וּא יַחְבֹּ֧ט יְהוָ֛ה מִשִּׁבֹּ֥לֶת הַנָּהָ֖ר עַד־נַ֣חַל מִצְרָ֑יִם וְאַתֶּ֧ם תְּלֻקְּט֛וּ לְאַחַ֥ד אֶחָ֖ד בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And it will be in the day the that, will beat out Yahweh from the flowing stream of the River to the wadi of Egypt, and you will be gathered one [by] one, sons of Israel.

en.L: And it will be in that day [that] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will beat out [grain] from the flowing stream of the River to the Wadi of Egypt, and you will be gathered one by one, {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel.
en.B: On that day {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will beat out the grain from the current of the Euphrates down to the Wadi of Egypt, and you will be picked up one at a time, {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}.
en.R: At that time {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will gather {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people the way a farmer beats grain from its stalks. He will do this in all the land from the Euphrates River to the stream at the border of Egypt. And you, people of Israel, will be gathered up one by one.

decisions.choice: beat out: threshing by beating, to collect every grain
alternatives: from the ears of grain of the River
decisions.reason: The verb is used for beating out grain or olives by hand (Judges 6:11; Ruth 2:17; Deuteronomy 24:20), so that nothing is lost. The word for "flowing stream" also means "ear of grain", which fits the picture of harvest.

decisions.choice: the River to the Wadi of Egypt: the full extent of the promised land
decisions.reason: "The River" is the Euphrates. The Wadi of Egypt is a stream bed in the desert at Egypt's border. Together they mark the bounds of the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18; 1 Kings 8:65).

decisions.choice: gathered one by one: gleaned like fallen grain
decisions.reason: The verb is used for gleaning, picking up grain left in a field (Ruth 2:2-3). God will not miss a single person of Israel.

decisions.choice: the grain; the Euphrates (Balanced and Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply the grain the verb implies and name the river.

decisions.choice: will gather his people the way a farmer beats grain
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of threshing as God's gathering of his people, which the end of the verse states.

source.text: וְהָיָ֣ה׀בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא יִתָּקַע֮ בְּשׁוֹפָ֣ר גָּדוֹל֒ וּבָ֗אוּ הָאֹֽבְדִים֙ בְּאֶ֣רֶץ אַשּׁ֔וּר וְהַנִּדָּחִ֖ים בְּאֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרָ֑יִם וְהִשְׁתַּחֲו֧וּ לַיהוָ֛ה בְּהַ֥ר הַקֹּ֖דֶשׁ בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And it will be in the day the that, will be blown on a trumpet great, and will come those lost in the land of Assyria and those banished in the land of Egypt, and they will bow down to Yahweh on the mountain of holiness in Jerusalem.

en.L: And it will be in that day [that] a great trumpet will be blown, and those perishing in the land of Assyria and those banished in the land of Egypt will come, and they will bow down to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.
en.B: On that day a great ram's horn will sound. Those lost in the land of Assyria will come, with those driven off into the land of Egypt, and they will bow down to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.
en.R: At that time someone will blow a loud trumpet. People who were lost in Assyria and people who were forced away to Egypt will come home. They will worship {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} holy mountain in Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: a great trumpet: the ram's horn, blown as a signal
decisions.reason: The instrument is a ram's horn, sounded to call people together or to announce a great day, as at the start of the Year of Jubilee, when people returned to their land (Leviticus 25:9-10; compare 18:3). Matthew 24:31 speaks of a loud trumpet when God's chosen are gathered.

decisions.choice: those perishing ... those banished: Israel's scattered people
decisions.reason: The first word means lost, wandering or perishing (Deuteronomy 26:5, "a wandering Aramean"); the second means driven out, as in 11:12. Assyria and Egypt stand for all the lands where Israel was scattered (11:11).

decisions.choice: they will bow down on the holy mountain: the return ends in worship
decisions.reason: The gathering ends at Zion, where the nations also come in 2:2-3 and where God holds his feast in 25:6.

decisions.choice: ram's horn (Balanced); trumpet (Literal and Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced names the instrument; Readable uses the familiar word.

decisions.choice: someone will blow; will come home; his holy mountain
decisions.reason: Readable turns the passive into an active sentence, says where the people come, and says whose mountain it is.
